messages.content:
You are checking a research plan against a list of experimental controls. You are not asked whether the plan is good. For each control of the list you give two separate answers: CONTENT (does the plan state this control?) and PLACE (is the passage written under an experiment that it can check?).

PLAN. A sequence of actions written one after the other by a planner. Each action adds or revises one proposed experiment and usually has the fields ACTION, TITLE, PROPOSAL, CONTROLS, COST and PREDICTION. Actions are separated by blank lines and are given in the order they were written. Every action counts, including an action that revises an earlier one and an action that looks incomplete.

REFERENCE CONTROLS. A list of experimental controls. Each has an identifier and a description.

CONTENT. Give exactly one content status for each reference control. Judge the content only, wherever the passage is written in the plan.
- "conforme": a passage of the plan states what the description requires (what is compared, held fixed, varied, repeated, measured or excluded). Different wording is fine. Nothing essential is missing or weakened.
- "altere": a passage of the plan states a recognisable but partial, vaguer, reduced or modified version of the control.
- "absent": no passage of the plan states this control.
If the control is stated in several places, keep the best content status found (conforme, then altere, then absent) and quote the passage that earns it. If several passages earn the same best status, quote one whose PLACE is "checks" if there is one.

PLACE. Only for "conforme" and "altere". Read the action that contains your quote, and judge it against the experiment that this action proposes (its TITLE and PROPOSAL), not against the description of the reference control. If that action has no TITLE and no PROPOSAL, answer "general" if the quoted control is general, otherwise "cannot_check".
- "checks": this experiment is one whose result the quoted control would check.
- "cannot_check": this experiment has nothing for the quoted control to compare, hold fixed, vary, repeat, measure or exclude.
- "general": the quoted control names no model, dataset, metric, quantity, condition or comparison that belongs to one experiment; it would apply to any experiment of the plan.
For "absent", PLACE is null. Your PLACE answer must never change your CONTENT answer.

Rules.
1. Judge each reference control on its own. One passage may support several controls.
2. Judge only what is written. Do not credit a control because it would be sensible, usual or implied. Do not lower a status for style, length, order or cost.
3. Evidence. For "conforme" and "altere", quote the passage that carries the control. Copy it character for character from a single action: no ellipsis, no added or removed word, no corrected spelling, no changed punctuation, no paraphrase. Take the shortest passage that is enough: at least 24 characters, at most 300 characters; if the whole field that carries the control is shorter than 24 characters, quote the whole field. A program searches the plan for your quote, word for word; a quote that is not found counts as "absent".
4. For "absent", the quote is null.
5. Give an answer for every reference control, and for no other identifier.

Answer with one JSON object and nothing else, in this form:
{"<identifier>": {"content": "conforme" | "altere" | "absent", "quote": "<quote>" | null, "place": "checks" | "cannot_check" | "general" | null}, ...}

PLAN
<<<
ACTION: add
TITLE: Effect of distilling into a 4-bit student on area under the detection curve for Pelleas-4
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Pelleas-4 on the Kettering proofs and measure area under the detection curve before and after distilling into a 4-bit student. The hypothesis is that distilling into a 4-bit student changes area under the detection curve on the Kettering proofs by more than run-to-run noise. We report area under the detection curve separately for short and long inputs of the Kettering proofs, since distilling into a 4-bit student may act differently on each. A secondary readout is median latency per query, reported on the held-out split of the Kettering proofs. We plan one pilot run on a tenth of the Kettering proofs to check that area under the detection curve is not saturated before the full experiment. We also evaluate transfer to the Wexcombe caption set without further tuning of Pelleas-4. We compare against Marrow-3, trained with the same budget on the Kettering proofs. The analysis is restricted to the examples of the Kettering proofs that Pelleas-4 answers correctly before the intervention.
CONTROLS: (1) Evaluate on the Wexcombe caption set as a held-out distribution. (2) Shuffle the labels of the Kettering proofs as a negative control for area under the detection curve. (3) Ablate distilling into a 4-bit student alone, keeping data and optimizer fixed, to isolate its effect on area under the detection curve. (4) Run Pelleas-4 on the Kettering proofs with five random seeds and report the spread of area under the detection curve. (5) Evaluate on the Wexcombe caption set as a held-out distribution.
COST: 35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: No change in area under the detection curve beyond seed noise on the Kettering proofs.

ACTION: add
TITLE: Effect of doubling the adapter rank on false-alarm rate at fixed recall for Quillon-L
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Quillon-L on the Halvard corpus and measure false-alarm rate at fixed recall before and after doubling the adapter rank. We compare against Sundrow-M, trained with the same budget on the Halvard corpus. The hypothesis is that doubling the adapter rank changes false-alarm rate at fixed recall on the Halvard corpus by more than run-to-run noise. All runs share one data order for the Halvard corpus, so that differences in false-alarm rate at fixed recall cannot come from batching. If false-alarm rate at fixed recall moves while exact-match accuracy stays flat, we attribute the change to doubling the adapter rank rather than to capacity. We also evaluate transfer to the Osric code suite without further tuning of Quillon-L. A secondary readout is exact-match accuracy, reported on the held-out split of the Halvard corpus. The analysis is restricted to the examples of the Halvard corpus that Quillon-L answers correctly before the intervention.
CONTROLS: (1) Evaluate on the Osric code suite as a held-out distribution. (2) Include Sundrow-M as a baseline under the same training budget. (3) Report exact-match accuracy on the Halvard corpus to check that the gain is not an artifact of one metric. (4) Shuffle the labels of the Halvard corpus as a negative control for false-alarm rate at fixed recall. (5) Run Quillon-L on the Halvard corpus with five random seeds and report the spread of false-alarm rate at fixed recall.
COST: 32 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: No change in false-alarm rate at fixed recall beyond seed noise on the Halvard corpus.

ACTION: add
TITLE: Effect of truncating the context to 2,000 tokens on pass rate on hidden tests for Halden-S
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Halden-S on the Pryce reasoning chains and measure pass rate on hidden tests before and after truncating the context to 2,000 tokens. If pass rate on hidden tests moves while mean token overlap stays flat, we attribute the change to truncating the context to 2,000 tokens rather than to capacity. We compare against Tessel-9, trained with the same budget on the Pryce reasoning chains. We report pass rate on hidden tests separately for short and long inputs of the Pryce reasoning chains, since truncating the context to 2,000 tokens may act differently on each. We plan one pilot run on a tenth of the Pryce reasoning chains to check that pass rate on hidden tests is not saturated before the full experiment. Each configuration of Halden-S is trained for the same number of steps and evaluated at three checkpoints. A secondary readout is mean token overlap, reported on the held-out split of the Pryce reasoning chains.
CONTROLS: (1) Shuffle the labels of the Pryce reasoning chains as a negative control for pass rate on hidden tests. (2) Repeat the evaluation of pass rate on hidden tests on the Pryce reasoning chains with a second prompt template. (3) Shuffle the labels of the Pryce reasoning chains as a negative control for pass rate on hidden tests. (4) Match the number of training steps between Halden-S and Tessel-9. (5) Include Tessel-9 as a baseline under the same training budget.
COST: 34 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Pass rate on hidden tests degrades on the Brenna-QA set while it holds on the Pryce reasoning chains.

ACTION: add
TITLE: Effect of shuffling the few-shot examples on recall at 5 for Dromond-8
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Dromond-8 on the Lowick tabular benchmark and measure recall at 5 before and after shuffling the few-shot examples. We expect the effect of shuffling the few-shot examples to be smaller for Corvane-12 than for Dromond-8, because Corvane-12 was never exposed to the Tolwyn dialogue logs. A null result on recall at 5 would still be informative if calibration error on the Tolwyn dialogue logs also stays within its usual range. We compare against Corvane-12, trained with the same budget on the Lowick tabular benchmark. We plan one pilot run on a tenth of the Lowick tabular benchmark to check that recall at 5 is not saturated before the full experiment. If recall at 5 moves while calibration error stays flat, we attribute the change to shuffling the few-shot examples rather than to capacity. We report recall at 5 separately for short and long inputs of the Lowick tabular benchmark, since shuffling the few-shot examples may act differently on each.
CONTROLS: (1) Include Corvane-12 as a baseline under the same training budget. (2) Shuffle the labels of the Lowick tabular benchmark as a negative control for recall at 5. (3) Report calibration error on the Lowick tabular benchmark to check that the gain is not an artifact of one metric. (4) Ablate shuffling the few-shot examples alone, keeping data and optimizer fixed, to isolate its effect on recall at 5. (5) Match the number of training steps between Dromond-8 and Corvane-12.
COST: 35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Recall at 5 degrades on the Tolwyn dialogue logs while it holds on the Lowick tabular benchmark.

TITLE: Effect of ablating the retrieval head on edit distance to the reference for Brindle-XL
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Brindle-XL on the Marisol summaries and measure edit distance to the reference before and after ablating the retrieval head. All runs share one data order for the Marisol summaries, so that differences in edit distance to the reference cannot come from batching. We expect the effect of ablating the retrieval head to be smaller for Ostrava-7 than for Brindle-XL, because Ostrava-7 was never exposed to the Avenel retrieval pool. We also evaluate transfer to the Avenel retrieval pool without further tuning of Brindle-XL. A secondary readout is agreement with the reference labels, reported on the held-out split of the Marisol summaries. Each configuration of Brindle-XL is trained for the same number of steps and evaluated at three checkpoints. A null result on edit distance to the reference would still be informative if agreement with the reference labels on the Avenel retrieval pool also stays within its usual range.
CONTROLS: (1) Include Ostrava-7 as a baseline under the same training budget. (2) Evaluate on the Avenel retrieval pool as a held-out distribution. (3) Ablate ablating the retrieval head alone, keeping data and optimizer fixed, to isolate its effect on edit distance to the reference. (4) Match the number of training steps between Brindle-XL and Ostrava-7. (5) Report agreement with the reference labels on the Marisol summaries to check that the gain is not an artifact of one metric.
COST: 29 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Edit distance to the reference improves by a small but reliable margin on the Marisol summaries.
